title: Static Timing Analysis
description: Setup and hold, slack and the critical path, clock skew and jitter, and how designers fix timing violations, with worked numeric examples.

lessons.title: Setup and Hold Times
objectives: Explain what happens on a violation
Say which clock edge each refers to
lessons.body:
A flip-flop samples its data input on the active clock edge. For that sample to be reliable the data must be stable for a short time before the edge, called the setup time, and for a short time after the edge, called the hold time.

If data changes inside this window, the flip-flop can capture a wrong value or enter a metastable state where its output is undefined for a while. Both numbers come from the cell library and depend on the device and conditions.

Setup is checked against the next clock edge: the data launched by one flip-flop must arrive before the following edge minus the setup time. Hold is checked against the same edge: the new data must not arrive so early that it changes before the hold time has passed. Static timing analysis checks both for every path without needing simulation vectors.

definitions.meaning: How long data must be stable before the clock edge.
How long data must stay stable after the clock edge.
An unresolved flip-flop state after a timing violation.
Checking all timing paths without simulating test vectors.

lessons.diagram:
clk   ___|-----|___
               ^ edge
  data  ====XXXX====
         <ts> | <th>
  stable: ts before, th after
mistakes: Thinking hold depends on the clock period: it does not, so slowing the clock does not fix hold violations.
Mixing up the edges: setup is for the next capture edge.
Ignoring metastability when crossing clock domains.

practice.q: Which time is measured before the edge?
Does reducing the clock frequency fix a hold violation?
practice.a: No, hold does not depend on the clock period.

exercises: Draw a timing sketch marking setup and hold around a rising edge.
Explain why STA does not need test vectors.
summary: Setup is before the edge, hold is after.
Violations can cause wrong or metastable values.

lessons.title: Clock Period, Slack and the Critical Path
objectives: Compute the minimum clock period for a path
Convert a period into a maximum frequency
lessons.body:
Consider two flip-flops with logic between them. After the launch clock edge the data needs the clock-to-Q delay (tcq) to leave the first flip-flop, then the combinational logic delay, and it must arrive at least the setup time (tsu) before the next edge. So in the simplest case (no skew) the clock period must satisfy T >= tcq + tlogic + tsu.

Slack is the margin: setup slack = T - (tcq + tlogic + tsu). Positive slack means the path meets timing. Negative slack is a violation. The path with the smallest slack is the critical path, and it limits the clock frequency of the whole design: fmax = 1 / Tmin.

definitions.meaning: Delay from the clock edge to a valid output of the launching flip-flop.
Timing margin: required time minus arrival time.
The path with the least slack.
Maximum clock frequency, 1 divided by the minimum period.

lessons.example:
tcq = 0.5 ns, tlogic = 3.2 ns, tsu = 0.3 ns
Tmin = 0.5 + 3.2 + 0.3 = 4.0 ns
fmax = 1 / 4.0 ns = 250 MHz
T = 5.0 ns -> slack = 5.0 - 4.0 = +1.0 ns
T = 3.5 ns -> slack = 3.5 - 4.0 = -0.5 ns (violation)
lessons.exampleNote: The path needs 4.0 ns. A 5 ns clock leaves 1 ns of margin; a 3.5 ns clock is 0.5 ns too fast.
lessons.diagram:
FF1 --tcq--> [ logic 3.2 ] --> FF2
  |<-- 0.5 -->|<--- 3.2 --->|<-0.3->|
  launch edge        next edge - tsu
  total required = 4.0 ns
mistakes: Forgetting clock-to-Q or setup time when adding up a path.
Reading a negative slack as good: negative means violation.
Computing fmax from the average path rather than the slowest.

practice.q: What is Tmin if tcq=0.4, tlogic=2.0 and tsu=0.2 ns?

practice.a: The critical path, the one with least slack.

exercises: Compute the slack at a 3 ns clock for the example path.
Find fmax for a path of tcq 0.3, logic 1.5 and tsu 0.2 ns.
summary: Slack = T minus the path requirement.

lessons.title: Clock Skew and Jitter
objectives: Adjust setup and hold checks for skew
lessons.body:
Clock skew is the difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops. Jitter is the cycle-to-cycle variation of the clock edge. Tools add an uncertainty margin to cover both.

Skew changes the checks. Let s be how much later the capture clock arrives than the launch clock. Setup becomes T >= tcq + tlogic + tsu - s, so positive skew helps setup. Hold becomes tcq + tlogic(min) >= th + s, so the same skew hurts hold.

Example: tcq = 0.4 ns, minimum logic delay = 0.1 ns, th = 0.2 ns, s = 0.4 ns. Data arrives after 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.5 ns, but must wait until 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6 ns, so hold slack is -0.1 ns: a violation. Designers balance the clock tree, and may use useful skew carefully.

definitions.meaning: Difference in clock arrival times at two flip-flops.
Variation of the clock edge position from cycle to cycle.
Buffered network that distributes the clock to all flip-flops.
Deliberately delaying a clock to borrow time for a slow path.

lessons.example:
Hold check with skew s = 0.4 ns:
  arrival   = tcq + tmin = 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.5 ns
  required  = th + s     = 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6 ns
  hold slack = 0.5 - 0.6 = -0.1 ns (violation)
lessons.exampleNote: The data changes 0.1 ns too early. Fix it by adding delay to the short path or by reducing skew.
lessons.diagram:
launch  clk _|---|___
  capture clk ___|---|__
  (capture later by skew s)
  new data must arrive AFTER
  capture edge + hold time
mistakes: Assuming skew always hurts: positive skew helps setup but hurts hold.

practice.q: Does positive skew help or hurt setup?
practice.a: It helps setup, giving the data more time.
Cycle-to-cycle variation in the clock edge timing.

exercises: Recompute the hold slack if the skew drops to 0.2 ns.
Explain why a balanced clock tree is usually the goal.
summary: Skew shifts setup and hold in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Fixing Setup and Hold Violations
lessons.body:
Setup violations mean a path is too slow. Typical fixes are to restructure or simplify the logic, upsize or buffer cells on long wires, move registers across logic (retiming), or add a pipeline stage. As a last resort you can lower the clock frequency.

Example: a path with tcq 0.5, logic 3.2 and tsu 0.3 ns needs 4.0 ns (250 MHz). Splitting the logic into two stages of 1.6 ns each gives 0.5 + 1.6 + 0.3 = 2.4 ns, about 416.7 MHz. The price is one extra cycle of latency and extra registers.

Hold violations mean a path is too fast. Slowing the clock does not help. The usual fix is to insert delay cells or buffers on the short path. Hold fixing is normally done late in the flow, after the clock tree is built.

definitions.meaning: Splitting logic into stages separated by registers.
Moving registers across logic to balance stage delays.
A buffer inserted to slow a path for hold fixing.
Number of cycles between input and output.

lessons.example:
Before: Tmin = 0.5 + 3.2 + 0.3 = 4.0 ns -> 250 MHz
After 2 stages of 1.6 ns:
  Tmin = 0.5 + 1.6 + 0.3 = 2.4 ns -> 416.7 MHz
Throughput up 1.67x, latency 1 extra cycle
lessons.exampleNote: Pipelining shortens the longest stage, so the clock can be faster, at the cost of one more cycle of delay.
lessons.diagram:
before: FF -[ 3.2 ns ]- FF
  after:  FF -[1.6]- FF -[1.6]- FF
  setup fix: shorten the path
  hold fix : lengthen the path
mistakes: Trying to fix hold by slowing the clock: it has no effect on hold.
Pipelining without adjusting dependent logic or latency.
Adding delay to a path that also has a setup problem.

practice.q: Name two ways to fix a setup violation.
practice.a: For example pipelining and restructuring or upsizing the logic.

practice.q: How do you fix a hold violation?
practice.a: Add delay (buffers or delay cells) on the short path.

exercises: Pipeline a path of 5.0 ns logic into two equal stages and compute the new Tmin with tcq 0.5 and tsu 0.3.
Explain why hold fixing waits until after clock-tree synthesis.
summary: Setup: make paths faster or add a stage.
